procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The Trial Court dismissed the suit. The First Appellate Court affirmed the decree of the Trial Court. The High Court affirmed the decree of the Trial Court.

issue.issue_text: Whether a Hindu female's property, in which she had a pre-existing limited interest under the Hindu Women's Rights to Property Act, 1937, is governed by Section 14(2) of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, thereby remaining a restricted estate, because her share was subsequently separated by an arbitration award.

facts: A Hindu widow inherited a share in her deceased husband's property under the Hindu Women's Rights to Property Act, 1937.
This 1937 Act granted her a limited interest, known as a "Hindu woman's estate," but also gave her the right to claim partition.
Before the Hindu Succession Act of 1956 came into force, an arbitration award was made which separated her share from the rest of the family property.
The award specified that her interest in the allotted property was a limited "widow's estate."
law: Section 14(1) of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, states that any property possessed by a female Hindu, whether acquired before or after the Act, shall be held by her as a full owner, not a limited owner.
The Explanation to Section 14(1) clarifies that 'property' includes that which is acquired at a partition.

Section 14(2) is an exception to Section 14(1). It states that Section 14(1) does not apply to property acquired under an award (or other instrument) if the terms of that award prescribe a restricted estate.
The Court interpreted Section 14(2) as applying only when a female acquires a right to property *for the first time* through an instrument like an award, without having any pre-existing right to it.
application: The Court determined that the widow's right to the property did not originate from the arbitration award. Her right was a *pre-existing right* that she had already acquired under the 1937 Act.
The arbitration award did not create a new right for her; it merely separated and quantified the share she was already entitled to as part of a partition.
Because the widow had a pre-existing right and was 'possessed' of the property when the 1956 Act came into force, her situation fell directly under Section 14(1).
The exception in Section 14(2) was deemed inapplicable because the award was not the source of her acquisition of the property; it was merely the mechanism for partitioning a right she already held.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the argument that the widow's property was governed by Section 14(2). The Court held that because the widow had a pre-existing right to the property under the 1937 Act, the subsequent arbitration award that merely partitioned her share did not bring the case within the exception of Section 14(2). Therefore, under Section 14(1) of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, her pre-existing limited interest was enlarged into a full and absolute ownership.

arguments.issue_text: Whether a Hindu female's property, in which she had a pre-existing limited interest under the Hindu Women's Rights to Property Act, 1937, is governed by Section 14(2) of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, thereby remaining a restricted estate, because her share was subsequently separated by an arbitration award.
appellant_arguments: The respondent acquired the property under the arbitration award or the subsequent court decree, not through a pre-existing right.
The award explicitly stated that the respondent would have a "widow's estate," which is a restricted estate.
Because the property was acquired under an award that prescribed a restricted estate, the case falls squarely under Section 14(2) of the Hindu Succession Act, making Section 14(1) inapplicable.
Section 14(2) should be read first as an exception, and only if it does not apply should Section 14(1) be considered.
respondent_arguments: The respondent already had a pre-existing interest and a right to partition in her husband's properties under the Hindu Women's Right to Property Act, 1937.
The arbitration award did not create a new right; it only separated her pre-existing share by metes and bounds.
The property was acquired "at a partition" as described in the Explanation to Section 14(1), which enlarges a pre-existing limited interest into a full one.
Since she was possessed of the property (in which she had a pre-existing right) when the 1956 Act came into force, her limited ownership became full ownership by virtue of Section 14(1).

statutes.act_name: Hindu Women's Right to Property Act, 1937 (Act XVIII of 1937)

cases.principle: Section 14(2) of the Hindu Succession Act clarifies that the purpose of Section 14 was to remove the legal disability imposed on women, not to interfere with rights restricted by contracts, grants, or decrees.

cases.case_name: Sukhram & Another v. Gauri Shankar & Another
cases.principle: A female Hindu who acquired a limited interest in joint family property under the Hindu Women's Right to Property Act, 1937, becomes a full owner of that property by virtue of Section 14(1) of the Hindu Succession Act.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: Section 14(2) of the Hindu Succession Act is a proviso or exception to Section 14(1) and only comes into operation if a female Hindu acquires property for the first time through an instrument such as a gift, will, decree, or award, without any pre-existing right to the property. Where a female Hindu has a pre-existing right or interest in a property, and an instrument such as a partition award merely separates or defines that share, her case is governed by Section 14(1), and she becomes the full owner.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: Sub-section (2) of Section 14 of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, is a proviso or exception to sub-section (1) and only applies when a property is acquired for the first time under one of the specified instruments (like an award) without the female having any pre-existing right. Where a Hindu female already has a pre-existing limited interest in a property, such as the one acquired under the Hindu Women's Rights to Property Act, 1937, a subsequent arbitration award that merely separates her share by metes and bounds does not constitute a new grant of property. Instead, her pre-existing limited ownership is enlarged into a full ownership by the operation of Section 14(1) of the 1956 Act.
legal_tests_applied: To determine if Section 14(2) applies, the court must ascertain if the property was acquired for the first time under the specified instrument (gift, will, decree, award etc.) without any pre-existing right in the female Hindu who is in possession of the property.
Section 14(2) is to be read as a proviso or exception to Section 14(1), not as the primary provision to be considered first.
why_appellant_lost: The appellant's argument to read Section 14(2) first as an exception was rejected as a "manner of reading of the section is not warranted either on principle or authority."

The court found that the arbitration award did not create a new right in the respondent for the first time; she already had a pre-existing interest under the 1937 Act. Therefore, the condition for applying Section 14(2) was not met.

The mere fact that a partition was effected by an arbitration award which resulted in a decree does not bring the matter within sub-section (2), especially when the Explanation to sub-section (1) expressly includes property acquired 'at a partition'.
why_respondent_won: The respondent had a pre-existing right in the properties under the Hindu Women's Right to Property Act, 1937, before the arbitration award was made.
The arbitration award did not create a new title but "had simply separated her share by metes and bounds."

Because the respondent had a pre-existing limited interest and was possessed of the property, her case fell squarely under Section 14(1), which enlarged her estate into a full ownership when the 1956 Act came into force.

The court found the case to be directly supported by precedent, specifically *Sukhram & Another v. Gauri Shankar & Another*, which held that a limited interest acquired under the 1937 Act becomes a full ownership under Section 14(1).
policy_considerations: The object of Section 14 was "only to remove the disability on women imposed by law and not to interfere with contracts, grants or decrees etc. by virtue of which a women's right was restricted" when that right was created for the first time by such an instrument.
